strongest_valid_partial_result: A rigorous proof that if mu(pi)<5/2 then the Flint-Hills series converges, and that mu(pi)>5/2 implies it diverges, via a correct dyadic level-set argument.
fatal_gaps: The candidate explicitly disclaims the target result: 'I cannot resolve either question. Both are open problems' — the exact target mu(pi)=2 is not proved.
The unconditional work stalls at mu(pi)<=11.842 via Beukers' zeta(2) integral plus the factor-2 transfer mu(pi)<=2 mu(pi^2); the manuscript itself abandons the claimed mu(pi)<=20 route mid-argument.
The transfer lemma mu(pi^2)=mu(pi) is attempted, found to be non-elementary, and replaced only by the lossy factor-2 sandwich; no repair is given.
The Zeilberger-Zudilin bound mu(pi)<=7.1032... is cited but explicitly not reproved, and in any case 7.1>5/2 so it cannot yield Flint-Hills convergence.
No construction (e.g., of the official paper's type) producing the optimal exponent 2 is present anywhere.
evidence_quotes: Final Claim. I cannot resolve either question. Both are open problems.
The series sum_n n^{2nu-5} converges iff 2nu-5<-1, i.e., nu<2. But we only have nu>mu(pi)>=2! So this direct term-by-term comparison fails
So I have rigorously proved mu(pi)<=11.842 from first principles via Beukers. This is my unconditional proved bound.
notes: The candidate is an honest, largely careful partial manuscript: after catching and fixing an initial error in the term-by-term estimate, it gives a correct and essentially complete dyadic proof of the sharp conditional threshold (mu(pi)<5/2 implies Flint-Hills converges; mu(pi)>5/2 implies divergence), which is a genuinely nontrivial rigorous partial result. However, against the exact target statement mu(pi)=2 it is in the wrong direction: it declares the problem open, proves only mu(pi)<=11.842 unconditionally (with the mu(pi^2)=mu(pi) transfer left unresolved and replaced by a lossy factor 2), and never attempts the optimal-exponent construction. Score 3 for the substantial correct conditional theorem; no credit toward the main theorem.
